claim: Iron accumulation can lead to oxidative stress and cellular death.
source: Iron is an essential molecule for biological processes, but its accumulation can lead to oxidative stress and cellular death.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental support in this manuscript.

claim: Iron accumulation is implicated in the process of aging and neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Due to its oxidative effects, iron accumulation is implicated in the process of aging and neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental support in this manuscript.

claim: Ferrous iron is the major form of iron used in mammalian cells.

source: The significance of sole increase in cytosolic iron is not clear, but the increase in mitochondrial iron in the brain is significant since it likely contributes to the oxidative damage that occurs in this tissue with aging.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed data and established knowledge about mitochondrial iron and oxidative damage.

claim: Cytosolic iron accumulation in the liver and muscle tissue may be due to mild increased systemic iron.
source: It is also possible that cytosolic iron accumulation in the liver and muscle tissue is due to mild increased systemic iron.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying cytosolic iron accumulation in liver and muscle.

claim: Iron accumulation in the brain with aging is likely independent of systemic iron metabolism.
source: Since the brain is not an iron storage organ and iron movement to the brain has to go through the blood-brain barrier (BBB), iron accumulation in the brain with aging is likely independent of systemic iron metabolism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known properties of the brain and blood-brain barrier.

claim: Clinical studies support targeting brain iron with iron chelators that can cross the BBB for neurodegenerative diseases associated with aging.
source: There is currently interest in taking the first approach and clinical studies support this approach (Sun et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sun et al., 2018.

claim: Targeting hepcidin in the brain is technically challenging and may require the design of small molecule hepcidin inhibitors that can also cross the BBB.
source: However, targeting hepcidin in the brain is technically challenging and may require the design of small molecule hepcidin inhibitors that can also cross the BBB.
evidence: This is speculation about potential therapeutic approaches.

claim: The study does not identify the specific cells in the brain that express hepcidin and FPN1.
source: We also acknowledge that we do not identify the specific cells in the brain that express hepcidin and FPN1.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the study.

claim: Identification of pathways involving brain-derived hepcidin regulation, Fpn1 expression, and iron accumulation may have therapeutic potentials.
source: Identification of these pathways may have therapeutic potentials.
evidence: This is speculation about potential therapeutic implications.

claim: UM-HET3 mice are a genetically heterogeneous mouse model that is the first-generation offspring of a CByB6F1 × C3D2F1 cross.
source: Tissues of liver, gastrocnemius muscle, and dissected brain cortex from young (4 months old) and aged (22 months old) female UM-HET3 mice, which is a genetically heterogeneous mouse model that is the first-generation offspring of a CByB6F1 × C3D2F1 cross to produce a diverse heterogeneous population in the Interventions Testing Program (ITP; https://www.nia.nih.gov/research/dab/interventions-testing-program-itp) (Harrison et al., 2021), were used in the present study.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Harrison et al., 2021.

claim: Mice were given diet Purina 5LG6 containing 345 ppm iron, which is similar to the published normal iron diet.
source: Mice were given diet Purina 5LG6 containing 345 ppm iron, which is similar to the published normal iron diet (Gutschow et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gutschow et al., 2015.
